Tuning the Electrocatalytic Properties of a Cu Electrode with Organic Additives Containing Amine Group for CO2 Reduction Yanling Qiua,Hexiang Zhonga,b, Wenbin Xua, Taotao Zhanga,c, Xianfeng Lia,b*and Huamin Zhanga,b*
The conversion of CO2 into value-added chemicals by employing renewable energy through an electrochemical process has received more and more attention. However, the low reaction rate and efficiency as well as poor selectivity limit its further development. The low CO2 solubility in aqueous solution is one of the main factors limiting the reaction rate and selectivity of CO2 electroreduction (ERC) under high overpotential. In this work, organic additive with –NH2 group (methyl carbamate, MC) has been incorporated into the ERC electrolyte for the first time. By utilizing the affinity interaction between the Lewis acid (the −NH3+ group of the protonated −NH2) and the Lewis base (CO2), the ERC reaction rate can be improved by 17%, and the Faradaic efficiency for CH4 can achieve 81.6%, which presents a high increment of 34% and has surpassed most of the reported Cu electrodes. Furthermore, the partial current density of CH4 is 31 mA cm-2 under –2.13 V (vs. RHE), which shows an increment of 30% when compared with that in the blank system. In addition, the competitive hydrogen evolution reaction can be prominently inhibited from 38.5% to 48.1% when the potential decreases gradually from –1.63 V to –1.98 V (vs. RHE). DFT calculations further indicate that the –NH3+ can prominently promote the adsorption of the CO* and CHO* on Cu surface and increase the surface coverage of both intermediates. The CHO* can be further stabilized by the −NH3+ group through facilitating partial electron transfer from Cu to C and formation of H-bond formation, which is favorable for the further hydrogenation to form hydrocarbons. These results provide a simple and powerful way to enhance the reaction rate and product selectivity for CO2 reduction.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
In the near two centuries, the reduction of CO2 into useful chemicals by employing renewable energy through an electrochemical process becomes more and more popular due to its advantages of high conversion efficiency and low cost.1 As one kind of products of the electroreduction of CO2 (ERC), hydrocarbons have been highly preferred due to their high energy density. Among all the metal catalysts reported since the pioneering work performed by Hori in 1985,2 copper is the only efficient metal electrocatalyst which can convert CO2 to hydrocarbons in aqueous solution.3,4 However, its low electrocatalytic activity and efficiency as well as poor hydrocarbon selectivity limit its further practical application.5,6
To improve the electrocatalytic activity and hydrocarbon selectivity of Cu electrode toward ERC reaction, a variety of methods have been proposed, including oxidized-derived (OD) Cu nanostructure,7-12 high dispersible Cu nanofilms,13 plasma-
activation to Cu foil,14,15 introducing additives to Cu surface or into the supporting electrolyte,16,17 generating stepped facet to Cu crystals3,18,19 or creating high-energy facets on Cu nanocrystals.20 These methods have greatly extended the electrochemical reaction area and improved the ERC reaction rate by increasing the surface roughness over the bulk copper electrode. At the same time, the selectivity for hydrocarbons can be significantly improved through regulating the exposure facet ratios and oxygen content on the surface and sub-layer. Experimental studies and theoretical calculations with single crystal Cu-electrodes have both revealed that Cu (111) basal plane leads to remarkable formation of CH4, while introduction of step sites to the Cu (100) basal plane leads to prominently enhanced formation of C2H4.21,22 Up to date, the highest faradaic efficiencies (FE) for methane and ethylene reported was ca. 85% and 70% over copper electrodes, respectively, and the partial current densities of CH4 and C2H4 was 38 mA cm-2 19 and 70 mA cm-2,23 respectively.
For ERC reaction, CO2 concentration in the electrolyte is an important factor influencing the ERC reaction rate and the product selectivity.24-26 A low CO2 solubility in aqueous solution (0.033 mol dm-3 at 25 oC),27 usually correlating with a higher mass transfer polarization, which has a negative effect on the ERC reaction, especially at a higher rate or for a rougher surfaces with larger area.7,14 In general, a serious mass transfer polarization results in a poorer ERC reaction efficiency and a higher hydrogen evolution reaction (HER).

Based on the DFT calculation, it is known that the energy barrier of the critical step is important for the eletrocatalytic activity of ERC reaction, and the adsorption strength of the key intermediates (such as COOH*, CO* and CHO*) on the catalyst active sites mainly determines the product selectivity.21,22,28-33 An ideal catalyst should bind with the intermediates appropriately, not too strongly, nor too weakly.34 In general, the binding energy of a molecule or an atom to a catalyst highly depends on the structure and composition as well as the environment of the surface.29 If some kinds of adsorbents can change the surface state of the catalyst, such as the charge distribution of the active sites, the binding energy of the intermediates on catalyst can be changed, and the surface’s catalytic performance and the products can be consequently modified.35
It is well known that a catalyst surface could be modified with functional additives by directly altering the electronic properties, or by indirectly affecting the binding strengths via adsorbateadsorbate interactions. For example, functionalized Au electrodes fabricated in an plating solution containing CN− or Cl− have been proved to be able to improve the ERC activity in comparison to pristine Au.36 Ag nanoparticles with different anchoring agents on carbon supports have been reported to lower the ERC overpotential and increase CO selectivity.37,38 Cu electrodes modified with amino acid exhibited remarkabley improved hydrocarbon generation and selectivity.16 Adsorbed halide anions on the Cu surface have been shown to facilitate the electron transfer at the interface by quickly stabilizing the adsorbed ERC intermediates.17 Although additives have been commonly used in the electrocatalyst preparation process, however, as far as we know, organic additives have seldom been involved in the electrolyte of ERC research. Through comparison of CO2 solubility in aqueous and organic solvents, it can be easily inferred that CO2 is more prone to be dissolved in organic solvents. For example, CO2 solubility in methanol and methyl acetate (MA) is about 2.6 times and 6.5 times higher than that in aqueous solution (Table S1).27
Inspired by this suggestion, in this paper, methyl carbamate (MC) was introduced into 0.5 M NaHCO3 aqueous solution as an organic additive for the first time to tune the electrochemical activity and the product selectivity of CO2 reduction. On the one hand, the −NH2 group in MC is prone to generate −NH3+ group (Scheme 1) in aqueous solution, and the affinity effect of the Lewis acid (−NH3+) with the Lewis base (CO2) can improve CO2 solubility (Table S1). Most importantly, the generated –NH3+ can prominently promote the adsorption of the CO* and CHO* on Cu surface and increase the surface coverage of both intermediates. Furthermore, The CHO* can be further stabilized by the −NH3+ group through facilitating partial electron transfer from Cu to C and formation of H-bond formation
Scheme 1.The MC promotion effect on CH4 generation
(Scheme 1), which is favorable for the further hydrogenation to form hydrocarbons along with their selectivity. Accordingly, there is an increment of 30% FE for CH4 and a decrement of 40% for the side effect of HER based on a 3 mM MC introduction. The result shows great potential of the organic additives for the application of the ERC system with aqueous electrolytes.

sections.heading: 2.1 Pretreatment of Cu electrode
sections.text: All the Cu foil (99.7%) electrodes were firstly dipped in acetone to remove the oil on the surface, and then chemically treated with concentrated hydrochloric acid to remove the oxidized Cu layer, and finally rinsed thoroughly with ultra-purity water and dried under inert gas atmosphere.

sections.heading: 2.2 MC and MA addition
sections.text: Different amount of MC powder was added to the solution to obtain electrolytes with different MC concentration (0.5 mM, 1 mM, 3 mM and 5 mM), and the related ERC reaction was referred as 0.5mM MC, 1mM MC, 3mM MC and 5mM MC, respectively. A certain amount of MA (Aladdin Industrial Corp., 99.5%) was added to the solution to obtain the electrolyte with 3 mM MA concentration. The ERC reaction in the electrolyte without addition was referred as Blank.

sections.heading: 2.3 ERC onset potential measuring
sections.text: The onset potential of ERC was studied by linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) in 0.5 M NaHCO3 solution saturated with high purity CO2 (99.999%) and N2 (99.999%). The corresponding instrument is a potentiostat (EG&G 2273, Princeton Applied Research). LSV curves were measured in the potential range from –0.6 V~ –2.65 V (vs. SCE) at a scan rate of 10 mV s-1. The initial LSV curve is the first cycle before the beginning of the ERC reaction, and the aft-LSV is the first cycle immediately at the end of the ERC reaction.

sections.heading: 2.4 Electrochemical impedance spectra testing
sections.text:
The EIS measurement was conducted by the electrochemical interface (Solartron S1 1287) and the Impedance/Gain-Phase Analyzer (Solartron S1 1260). The testing frequency is from 1 MHz to 1 Hz. The measurement was carried out in 0.5 M NaHCO3 aqueous solution under two limited condition: one is at the static state without stirring and with no CO2 continuing provision after the solution is saturated with CO2. The test is aiming to study the effect of CO2 capturing ability of MC or MA on the ohmic resistance and the charge transfer resistance of the ERC system under insufficient CO2 supply condition. The second one is measured at the state of adequate CO2 provision with strong agitation (500 rpm) and continuous CO2 bubbling into the electrolyte. By this simulation, the MC effect on the charge transfer resistance of ERC can be explored.
Zsimpwin simulating software was employed to fit the recorded plots and calculate the ohmic resistance and the charge transfer resistance. The fitting circuit is LR (CR).

sections.heading: 2.5 Electrocatalytic reduction of CO2
sections.text:
All CO2 electrochemical reduction experiments were conducted at atmospheric pressure and room temperature by a potentiostat (EG&G 2273, Princeton Applied Research) in a home-made H-type cell, which was composed of the cathodic and anodic compartment with a piece of Nafion®115 (Dupont) membrane sandwiching in the middle. Saturated calomel electrode (SCE, with saturated KCl as the filling solution) and platinum foil were used as the reference and counter electrodes, respectively. The measured electrode potential can be converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) reference scale using ERHE = ESCE + 0.242 V + 0.0591 × pH. No solution resistance was compensated in this work since the resistance of the 0.5 M NaHCO3 aqueous solution is relatively much lower than that in diluted one.4 The acidity or alkalinity of the solution was determined by a pH meter S210 (SevenCompact, Mettler Toledo) after CO2 bubbling at least 40 min.
The electrolyte was 0.5 M NaHCO3 saturated with CO2 (pH=7.2), and was stirred at a rate of 500 rpm during electrolysis. CO2 was continuously delivered into the cathodic compartment at a rate of 60 sccm. During the test, the cell outlet (consisting of residual CO2, and the gas-phase products) was on-line delivered directly into gas chromatography (GC2014, Shimadzu) which was equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and a hydrogen ionization flame detector (FID), a Porpack-N column and a Molecular Sieve-13X column to analyze and quantify gas products with 1.0 ml loop. Argon was used as the carrier gas.
The FE of ERC products were calculated on the basis of the transferred number of electrons for the formation of one molecule of the products from CO2 and H2O, i.e., 8 for CH4, 12 for C2H4. The partial current density of CH4 was calculated from the gas chromatograph peak areas as below.
Where α is the conversion factor for CH4 based on calibration of the gas chromatograph with standard samples, P0 = 101.3 kPa and T = 293.15 K, S is the electrode geometry area.
The total FE of the detected gas products, including H2, is in the range of 82%~110% (Figure S1a). In addition, a small amount of HCOOH was also detected (Figure S1b). However, the FE for HCOOH was less than 5% when the applied potential was negative than - 1.48V.

sections.heading: 2.6 Calculation details.
sections.text:
Our calculations were performed using the density functional theory (DFT) under the generalized gradients approximation (GGA),39 the revised Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (RPBE)40 exchange correlation functional, and the projector augmented wave (PAW) method,41 as implemented in the Vienna Ab initio Simulation
Package (VASP).42-44 The Cu (111) surfaces were chosen to model the experimental systems, because the Cu (111) surface is always considered as the preferential crystallographic orientation toward CH4 product.45 A 3×3×3 atom slabs of Cu (111) surface was employed with 15 Å of vacuum, while the bottom layer was fixed during the structure optimization calculations, using a 4×4×1 Monkhorst–Pack mesh of K-point sampling. All calculations were run in non-spin-polarized mode with plane-wave cutoff of 400 eV, and the maximum atomic force of 0.02 eV/AA was set as the convergence criterion for structure relaxation with 0.1 eV Fermilevel smearing. Herein, the adsorption energies are calculated as the difference between the total energies of the clean surface and the corresponding free adsorbate in the gas phase and the total energy of the adsorption system. The energies of C, H, and O atoms are referenced to graphene, gaseous hydrogen (H2), and the difference between water and hydrogen (H2O − H2). The slice of charge densities and Bader partial atomic charges were performed from the electron density as calculated from the self-consistent calculation of DFT, where the Self-consistent Calculation (SCF) convergence was set to 1 × 10−6 eV/atom to obtain more accurate ground state electron density and a finer FFT grid was used with the NGXF/NGYF/NGZF value of 180 to get accurate core charge during Bader calculation. Moreover, the slice of charge densities was visualized in VESTA software46 and Bader partial atomic charges were calculated using the Bader Charge Analysis code.47

sections.heading: 3.1 Effect of MC on the catalytic activity
sections.text:
To determine the effect of MC addition on ERC reaction rate and the activity sites over Cu surface, the intrinsic catalytic property of MC for ERC was investigated firstly with carbon paper as the electrode (Figure S2) in CO2 saturated 0.5 M NaHCO3 with or without MC addition. The completely coincidence of the LSV curves in different ERC systems (Figure S2a) implies that MC can’t inherently improve the activity of the ERC reaction. The rarely changed CH4 concentration and FE after MC incorporation further confirms that the MC has no activity on CH4 generation during ERC reaction (Figure S2b).
The linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) scans in CO2 saturated 0.5 M NaHCO3 with or without MC addition were measured before and after the ERC test (Figure 1). The onset potential (Eonset) of the ERC reaction is -0.3V and -0.35V, respectively, for the ERC system with and without MC addition. It indicates that the MC addition can slightly lower the overpotential of the ERC reaction while rarely change the active sites on Cu surface. However, in the low overpotential range (Figure 1a inset and 1c), the current in the MCadditive system is slightly lower than that in the blank system. As the HER prevails in this potential range,4 this result implies that MC molecules might cover on some active sites favoring HER reaction. It is worth to note that the cathode current shows a small decrease near −0.83 V and −1.18 V after the ERC test (Figure 1b), which corresponds to the reduction from CO2 to CO*, and the slightly

current drop is resulted from the blocking effect of surface active sites by the adsorbed CO*.48 In the ERC system with MC-addition, the positive shift of this peak potential means MC can promote CO2 being reduced to CO*, which would be realized by reducing the reaction free energy of CO2 reduction to CO* formation or by improving the binding strength of CO* on the Cu active sites.16 As the adsorbed CO* must be produced during the ERC process, it can be predicted that the shoulder should appear on each LSV curve after every ERC test, i.e., under any applied negative potential. Once sufficient desorption time (e.g. 2 hours) is provided, the adsorbed species on the Cu surface will disappear and the shoulder will not appear on the LSV curves. When the electrolysis potential is negative than −1.13 V, the current in MC addition system is higher than that in the blank system, and the increasing amplitude becomes more obvious with the potential shifting to more negative region. Under −1.98 V (vs. RHE), about 17% current gain is obtained in the MC-addition system (Figure 1d). This result suggests the catalytic activity of the electrochemical reduction reaction has been improved, both for the HER and ERC.
It is well known that the ERC reaction rate is proportional to CO2 concentration adjacent to the Cu electrode surface.24 The MC can capture CO2 molecules through the affinity effect of the Lewis acid (−NH3+) with the Lewis base (CO2). As the result, the current gain under high overpotential should be partially contributed to the catalytic improvement of Cu electrode due to the CO2 concentration increase.

sections.heading: 3.2 The product selectivity
sections.text:
To determine whether the current increase in Figure 1 is the
result of ERC reaction improvement or HER prevailing, the product selectivity after introducing MC, including FE and the partial current density of CH4, was detected and the result was shown in Figure 2.
The Cu electrode in this study is Cu (111) facet preferred (Figure S3 and Table S2), and the ERC reaction products are mainly hydrocarbons and H2 in the studied potentials (Figure S1), which can be attributed to the high NaHCO3 concentration in the electrolyte.19
Compared with the blank system, the Cu electrode in the MCaddition system demonstrates much higher selectivity toward hydrocarbons, especially for CH4. In Figure 2a, the advantage becomes more and more pronounced with the reduction potential shifting to more negative region. The FE for CH4 is more than 80% under –1.98 V, which is 34% higher than that in the blank system and has surpassed most of the reported Cu electrodes (whether modified on the Cu or in the supporting electrode, Table S3). Furthermore, MC addition also exhibits its beneficial effect on CH4 production rate (Figure 2b). The JCH4 reaches up to 31 mA cm-2, that is, a 30% higher than that in the blank system under −2.13 V (vs. RHE). These results hint that the introduction of MC in the electrolyte is favor of improving CH4 generation rate along with the selectivity on Cu electrodes. It is worthy to note from the comparative results of GC and Cu electrode in the MC-addition systems (Figure 2a and 2d) that the catalyst must be applied to reduce CO2 even under very high overpotentials, as the GC has almost no catalytic selectivity to the ERC products, and H2 nearly prevails in the tested potential window.
Apart from favoring CH4 generation, MC addition also facilitates to improve the C2H4 selectivity (Figure 2c). The FE for C2H4 in the MC-addition system is always higher than that in the blank system, and almost 2-fold higher even under −1.48 V. Another beneficial effect of MC addition is the significant prohibition of HER, which is reflected in Figure 2d and Table 1. The decline ratio of FE for H2 is increased from 38.5% to 48.1% compared with its counterpart, when the potential is decreased from −1.63 V to −1.98 V (vs. RHE).
Fig. 2 Comparison of ERC product selectivity on Cu electrode in ERC system with or without MC addition. a) FE for CH4, b) partial current density of CH4, c) FE for C2H4, d) FE for H2. The electrolyte is CO2 saturated 0.5 M NaHCO3 aqueous solution under ambient pressure.

The improved FE for CH4 and C2H4 as well as the inhibition of H2 is well in agreement with the LSV and chronoamperometry results, which well confirmed our idea of improving ERC reaction rate by increasing CO2 concentration adjacent to the reaction interface, and the product distributions can also be modulated by the introduction of appropriate organic additives.
As multistep reaction processes and a number of key intermediate species are involved (such as COOH*, CO*, CHO*, etc.) during hydrocarbons formation in ERC reaction,30 the selective improvement of hydrocarbons induced by MC addition should be correlated with the binding energy between some key intermediates and the catalytic active sites on Cu surface. It is well known that the most critical intermediates in CH4 production are CO* and CHO*,49 based on the results in Figure 2a), we speculate that MC addition might improve the adsorption strength of these two intermediates on Cu surface, which increases the probability of CH4 production. In addition, as C2H4 production mechanism also involves CO* generation,45 FE for C2H4 increase in Figure2c) also support the view of the adsorption strength improvement of CO* on the Cu electrode. In another hand, the H2 inhibition tendency implies that the bond strength of the Cu surface to proton might be increased with MC addition, which leads to the lower escape rate of H2 from Cu surface.

sections.heading: 3.3 The effect of MC concentration on product selectivity of ERC
sections.text:
In the ERC reaction system, MC molecules have two functions on the electrode surface. The first one is the adsorption effect, that is, MC molecules adsorb on the negative charged surface of copper electrode. The adsorption of MC on Cu surface will inevitably reduce the number of active sites involved in the electrochemical reaction. The second function is to improve the adsorption strength of the CO* and CHO* on Cu (111), and stabilize the CO* and CHO* species by the -NH2 group in MC structure and its protonation NH3+ group. The maximum selectivity of ERC products can be obtained when the two functions reach to a balance.
To investigate the effect of MC addition on the coverage of Cu active sites and ERC reaction rate as well as the product selectivity, the MC concentration should be optimized. Figure 3 gives the result of the effect of MC concentration on the static current and FE for CH4 as well as H2 under –1.98 V (vs. RHE). Both the current and FE for CH4 shows an inflection point with 3 mM MC addition, while the FE for H2 demonstrates an opposite variation. The positive effect
tends to be weakened as MC concentration is higher than 3 mM, indicating there is an optimum MC concentration for the CH4 selectivity in the ERC reaction. It is anticipated from Figure 3 that 3 mM MC addition can not only increase the binding strength between the key intermediates (such as CO* and / or CHO*) and the Cu surface, but also not notably decrease the total number of the effective active sites required for the electrochemical reaction. The effect of MC concentration on the electrocatalytic activity and product selectivity is consistent with the result of dynamic test before and after ERC reaction (Figure 1).

sections.heading: 3.4 Mechanism of MC addition on the improvement of ERC electrocatalytic activity and product selectivity
3.4.1 EIS spectrum
sections.text:
To explore the variation of the charge transfer process occurring at the Cu electrode/solution interface arising from MC addition, the electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) were measured and compared (Figure S4). In the ERC reaction system with sufficient CO2 supply (Figure S4a), the ohmic resistance (RΩ) decreased with a 19% decrement and Rct decreased nearly 56% for the system with MC addition when compared with the blank system (Table S4). It is known that the ohm resistance is mainly resulted from the solution, which accordingly will increase when large amount of small bubbles existing in solution. As MC addition can be effective to inhibit HER significantly (38% ~ 48%), much less H2 bubbles will be present in the electrolyte compared with that in the blank system. As a result, the ohmic resistance RΩ can be reduced due to the decreased electron transfer resistance. On the other hand, the strong interaction between CO* and CHO* on Cu surface with MC addition can prevent the escape of CO* and CHO* from the electrode, which is favorable for its further hydrogenation to form hydrocarbons. This process can facilitate the H+ transfer process, thus decrease the charge transfer resistance (Rct) compared with the blank system. Therefore, decrease of both RΩ and Rct means MC has a dualfunction of HER inhibition and charge transfer velocity increase, which is in agreement with the reaction rate enhancement (Figure 1d) and the improved hydrocarbon selectivity (Figure 2a and 2c). On the other hand, the RΩ and Rct with insufficient CO2 supply in MC-addition ERC system (Figure S4b) is ca. 13% and 21% lower than those in the Blank system. Compared with those in the sufficient CO2 supply system, less reduction extent of the resistances with

sections.heading: 3.4.2 The intrinsic driving force variation induced by MC addition (Tafel slope)
sections.text:
To further characterize the resistance of charge transfer in ERC system with MC addition, the partial current density of CH4 under lower overpotential range in CO2 saturated 0.5 M NaHCO3 solution with or without MC addition was measured, and the result was used to calculate Tafel slope. In general, the smaller the Tafel slope is, the smaller the resistance for the electron transfer will be, and the less overpotential is needed to drive the same electrochemical current. Previous studies indicate that CO2 reduction on copper foils proceeds with a first-order dependence on CO2 pressure in aqueous electrolytes,49,50 and the first one-electron step of CO2 to COOH* or CO2•− intermediates is determining the rate for the 8 electron transfer-combined process for CH4.51,52
The Tafel slope measured for Cu foil of 102 mV dec−1 in the blank system agrees well with the prior reports13,53 (86 mV dec−1 and 114 mV dec−1), whereas much lower Tafel slope of 63 mV dec−1 on Cu electrode toward CH4 formation (Figure 4) is obtained with 3 mM MC addition into the electrolyte, verifying the beneficial effect of CO2 concentration increase induced by MC addition, and suggesting a faster first-electron transfer step involved in CH4 generation.54 As the most critical intermediates of ERC in hydrocarbon production are CO* and CHO*,49 it is predicted that MC addition alters the adsorption strength of these intermediates on Cu surface.

sections.heading: 3.5 Effect of MC on the adsorption properties of CO* and CHO* to
Cu surface active sites
sections.text:
To further reveal the underlying mechanism of the MC effect on the selectivity improvement of CH4 and the increased electrocatalytic ERC activities, Cu-C bond length, hydrogen bond length as well as adsorption energies of CO* and CHO* were carried out with DFT calculations and the results are listed in Table 2. The adsorption configurations in DFT calculations are shown as Figure S5.
The adsorption energy of intermediate are defined as follows:
ECxHyOz = Etotal - Eslab- xEC - yEH –zEO (1)
where ECxHyOz, Eslab, EC, EH, and EO are the energy of the total system, the energy of the slab or the slab with additive molecules, and the energies of C, H, and O atoms, respectively. The difference of adsorption energies of CO* and CHO* on Cu surface with or without MC addition can be obtained from Table 2. In general, when the adsorption energy is positive, it means that the environment needs more energy for the system to ensure the particle adsorb on the electrode surface. The lower the adsorption energy is, the easier the adsorption of particles on the electrode surface will be. In Table 2, the adsorption energies of CO* and CHO* on Cu (111) are positive,
Fig. 4 Tafel curves comparison between ERC reaction systems with and without MC addition.
indicating both intermediates are difficult to adsorb on Cu (111). Specifically, the adsorption energy of CO* on the Cu electrode for the system with and without MC addition is 0.970 and 1.189 eV, respectively, corresponding to a decrease of 0.219 eV after the MC addition, suggesting less extra energy is needed to promote CO* adsorption on the Cu electrode after the MC addition. As for the adsorption energies of CHO*, the values of the adsorption energies are 1.246 eV and 1.832 eV, respectively, indicating the increased adsorption properties of CHO* on Cu surface with MC addition system. The easier adsorption of CO* and CHO* on Cu active sites in MC-additive system can improve the surface coverage of CO* and CHO* on Cu surface, which is favorable for their further hydrogenation to produce hydrocarbons.22 Compared with the – NH2 group in MC, its protonated –NH3+ exhibits stronger H-bond with both CO* and CHO* with the H-bond length decreasing 1 Å and 0.66 Å, respectively. This comparison in the H-bond length suggests the stabilization of CO* and CHO* in MC addition system. In addition, the −NH3+ group can further reduce the Cu-C bond length to about 0.5 Å and 0.03 Å, implying the stronger interaction between Cu surface and CO*/CHO*. On the other hand, for the ERC system with MC addition, the CHO* intermediate is much more easily formed from CO* intermediate (Table 3). The reaction heat from CO* to CHO* decreases from 0.644 eV to 0.491 eV and then to 0.276 eV, implying less heat is required to drive the reaction, especially in −NH3+ system. Therefore, the −NH3+ group introduced by the MC adsorbed on the Cu surface can promote the adsorption of CO* and CHO* on Cu surface, increase the surface coverage of both intermediates and facilitate CHO* formation, resulting in the enhanced hydrocarbon generation. These calculations provide theoretical support for the improvement of selectivity and product yield of hydrocarbons in the ERC system with MC addition.
To further verify MC effect on the stabilization of ERC key intermediates, the bader partial atomic charges were calculated using the Bader Charge Analysis Code (Figure 5). Considering the original valence charge for Cu C and O atom as 11, 4, and 6 respectively, it can be deduced that the Bader partial atomic

Specifically, compared with the blank system, the bader partial atomic charge on the carbon atom of CHO* has been increased from 2.487 to 2.589 and then to 2.718, then to 2.718, respectively, in the presence of MC and MC−NH3+, while those on Cu is decreased from 10.907 to 10.881 and then to 10.837, respectively. The amount of electron-charge donated is correlated with the number of Cu−C bonds formed between the C atom and Cu atoms on the surface,55 which is consistent with the results of Cu−C bond length in Table 2. In addition, the electron transfer between the entire intermediate and additive are also calculated with the following formula:
∆e(CHO)=e(Cu)+e(C)+e(H)+e(O)−22 (2)
where e(Cu), e(C), e(H), and e(O) are the bader charges in their respective system. The electron transfer of the entire intermediate (*CHO) is ∆e(NH3+−CHO, 0.229) > ∆e(Cu−CHO, 0.088), implying more electron transfer of the entire intermediate with MC-NH3+. On the other hand, the number of electrons in H1 is less than that in H2, indicating that some of the electrons in H1 are transferred to O in CHO* to form hydrogen bonds, which further increase the CHO* stability. These results imply that MC involvement could not only tune the electronic structure of the Cu surface, but also modulate the product selectivity through altering the adsorption strength of the key intermediates involved in the ERC reaction pathway.
To confirm the proton donation to the CHO from the –NH3+ group, ERC reaction has been carried out under various pHs. To avoid additional anion effect on the ERC reaction, the pH was tuned through the electrolyte concentration modification. The results are shown in Figure S6. When pKa increases from 6.4 to 7.6, the proton
Fig. 5 Slice of charge densities and Bader partial atomic charges are indicated in orange with and without MC.
concentration decreases about 15−fold. The FE for CH4 demonstrates volcano relations with the pH, and the highest selectivity appears at 7.2. Under lower pH, the proton concentration near the Cu surface is relatively higher, and the competitive adsorption of H* with CHO* is prominent. As a result, the proton donation to the CHO* from the NH3+ is relatively weak. The circumstance is adverse under higher pH, i.e., the proton concentration whether adjacent Cu surface or in the bulk solution is lower, the proton donation effect on the CHO* binding from the - NH3+ is correspondingly reduced. As CH4 formation strongly depends on the proton concentration, an increased pH would lead to lower CH4 formation. Therefore, the beneficial effect of MC addition on enhancing the ERC reaction rate and improving hydrocarbons selectivity are mainly concentrated in a narrow pH range.

sections.heading: 3.6 Distinguish the weight ratio of the CO2 concentration increase from the stabilization of MC to the key intermediates
sections.text:
To distinguish the effect of MC addition on CO2 concentration improvement from the ERC intermediates binding strength, a comparison experiment was carried out with −NH2 replaced by −CH3 group. Methyl acetate (MA) instead of MC was added into 0.5 M NaHCO3 solution. Both the dynamic current (Figure S7a) and static current (Figure S7b) increased evidently with MA addition, which is induced by the increased CO2 concentration. Improved CH4 selectivity and inhibited HER at a wide potential window (−1.23 V ~ −2.13 V) are also observed (Figure S8). The MA effect on the catalytic selectivity of ERC is close to that of MC, and the difference between the two additives is mainly reflected in more negative potentials (≤−1.8 V). Therefore, the beneficial effect of MC on the ERC electrocatalytic activity and hydrocarbon selectivity under higher overpotentials is the synergistic results of CO2 concentration improvement and the stabilization to the key intermediates. EIS results in ERC systems with or without sufficient CO2 supply also confirmed that MC has the dual effect of reducing the system resistance with MC affinity to CO2 and charge transfer resistance with their stabilized effect on the key intermediates (Figure S9), which are the primary contribution to hydrocarbon selectivity.

Through I-t curves (Fig. 1c, 1d), it can be seen that the currents with or without MC addition decreased with time to different degree, which means the activity of Cu electrode is not stable, even in the ERC system with MC addition. It is worthy to note that the MC molecule can still maintain its stability without degradation because of the reduction characteristic under the negative electrochemical potentials applied.
The stability of the electrode in the presence of MC includes two aspects: one is the stability under much more negative potentials, the other is the stability as the reaction time was prolonged under a specific potential. For the former case, there will be more negative charge on the electrode surface due to the more negative potentials, then, the binding energy of the key intermediates, such as CO*, will become stronger, leading to the difficult desorption of CO*, and the catalyst will be poisoned. As a result, the adsorption of other intermediate will be restrained, which could hinder the further hydrogenation or dimeration of CO*. For the latter case, the current decrease trend is correlated with CO* coverage variation on the Cu surface. It is reported that CO* can’t completely occupy the Cu surface at potentials relative to ERC reaction, thus leaving active sites for H* adsorption and C-H bond formation.56 In ERC system with MC addition, large part of CO* can be further hedrogenerated to CHO* or dimerization to OCCO intermediates, the CO* accumulation on Cu surface is slower than that without MC addition, and the total amount of the active sites on Cu surface is decreasing much slower due to the increased binding energy of CHO* with Cu (111). This speculation has been verified by the durability test and the result is demonstrated in Figure 6 and Figure S10 a). It can be observed from both figures that it require longer time in the MC addition system to enable the current decrease to the stable one (1.8h versus 0.2h), that is, MC addition can reduce the poison effect of Cu electrode in ERC reaction, but can’t absolutely inhibit its poison. As comparison, the FE for CH4 is almost totally lost within the initial 1h in MA-addition ERC system (Figure S10b), and H2 becomes prevailing concurrently, indicating that the catalytic performance of the Cu electrode in the MA-addition system isn’t improved at all. These results further confirm the beneficial effect of the additives with –NH2 group on the ERC reactions.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text: In this work, an organic additive with −NH2 group (MC) was introduced into the electrolyte of ERC reaction to enhance the electrocatalytic activity and hydrocarbons selectivity over Cu electrode. A remarkable enhancement (ca. 30%) in faradaic efficiency as well as partial current density of CH4 is obtained with an appropriate MC addition. MC addition would slightly increase the electrocatalytic activity of ERC and suppress H2 evolution by improving the CO2 concentration on the Cu electrode surface. Theoretical calculations disclose that the −NH2 group in the MC structure and its protonated −NH3+ group can promote the adsorption of CO* and CHO* on Cu surface, increase the surface coverage of both intermediates and facilitate CHO* formation. Furthermore, the CO* and CHO* on Cu (111) can be stabilized through facilitating partial electron transfer from Cu to C and formation of H-bond formation by the generated −NH3+ group, which is favorable for the further hydrogenation to form hydrocarbons. The results suggest that organic additives with −NH2 group are very promising for enhancing the ERC reaction rate and improving hydrocarbons selectivity.
